# Idempotent Teardown Scripts

Every script in the set can be run again, from any state, without editing it first. Not achieved by a
migration framework or a test harness — achieved by two rules applied by hand: **teardown swallows
"does not exist", and anything that writes data ends in `ROLLBACK`.**

The property is stated as a guarantee in the README, which is what makes it a pattern rather than an
accident:

> "Each script is idempotent: the teardown scripts swallow \"does not exist\", and every block that
> modifies data ends in `ROLLBACK`."
> — Oracle-Database-Laboratories/README.md, 2026-07-25

## The three mechanisms

**1. Drop child-first, in a declared order.** Both teardown scripts hold the object names in a nested
table in dependency order and loop over it, so no foreign key ever blocks a `DROP`. The
object-relational teardown has a second ordering rule on top, and states why the obvious shortcut is
wrong:

> "Object tables go before the types they are built on -- a type with a table depending on it cannot
> be dropped, and FORCE would leave the table invalid rather than removing the dependency."
> — Oracle-Database-Laboratories/sql/04_object_relational/00_drop_all.sql, 2026-07-25

**2. Swallow exactly two error codes, re-raise everything else.** The local `drop_object` procedure
catches `WHEN OTHERS`, allows `SQLCODE IN (-942, -4043)` — table/view does not exist, object does not
exist — and calls `RAISE` otherwise. That narrowness is the whole point: a blanket
`WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL` would make the script idempotent *and* blind. See
[[plsql-exception-handling]].

**3. Never commit.** Every exercise block that inserts, updates or fires a trigger ends in `ROLLBACK`,
and every trigger script drops the trigger and any scratch table it created before moving on. The
demonstration leaves the schema exactly as it found it, so the next script's assumptions still hold.

## Why it matters more here than a framework would

There is no test runner, no migration tool and no CI in [[oracle-database-laboratories]]. Re-runnable
scripts are the *entire* reproducibility story: a reader can execute the suite top to bottom, get the
documented result, and execute it again immediately. The property is structural rather than asserted
— it holds because of how the code is written, not because something checks it.

It also makes [[numbered-stages-in-directory-names]] safe. Numbered run order only helps if starting
over is cheap; if step 3 leaves committed rows behind, re-running step 1 is not a reset.

## The same instinct elsewhere in the source set

- [[idempotent-loading]] — `MERGE`-based Cypher import in the discrete-maths repo, re-runnable for
  the same reason and fixed by re-reading rather than rebuilding.
- [[etl-load-order]] — warehouse loads that must create before they load; the ordering half of the
  same problem, without the teardown half.

The distinctive move here is the **exception-code allow-list**. Both other instances get idempotency
from an upsert primitive the engine provides; this one gets it from deciding, explicitly, which two
failures mean "already in the desired state".

## Cost

The `ROLLBACK` discipline means the scripts can never be used to actually populate a working schema —
running `03_plsql/` leaves no data behind by design. Seeding is a separate step
(`01_schema/03_seed_data.sql`), and the split is invisible until someone runs the PL/SQL scripts
expecting persistence. Worth knowing before adapting any of it.
